idiom_name: non-virtual public entry point + non-public overridable hook
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep every published operation non-overridable (the language's own default, or an explicit final/non-open modifier), and put each customizable step in a single hook that is visible to subclasses and to nobody else (private where the language allows it, protected where subclasses must be able to implement it, documented convention where the language has no visibility at all). The entry point performs the invariant - pre/post-conditions, locking, logging, normalisation - and calls exactly one hook; the base class must never call its own published operations, or a subclass's hook runs twice. Document the hook contract (what it may assume, what it must guarantee) because non-public hooks are invisible in API listings.
code_sketch:
base.public_op(x):        # non-virtual entry point, written once
    check_pre(x)          # lock, validate, log
    result = hook(x)      # the only overridable step
    check_post(result)    # validate result, unlock
    return result
# concrete type implements hook(); it cannot restate public_op
pitfalls: Making the entry point overridable again (virtual, open, non-final, or hidden by a derived overload set) recreates the hole the pattern closes.
Calling a hook from a constructor or destructor dispatches to a subtype that is not fully constructed or is already destroyed.
One entry point calling another entry point runs the hooks twice and silently breaks subclasses (fragile base class).
Wrong move: Expose the hook as public -> clients bypass validation, locking, or accounting -> instead keep it private/protected and route calls through the wrapper.

Wrong move: Call a hook from a constructor or destructor -> virtual dispatch sees an incomplete or already-torn-down subtype -> instead use non-virtual initialization/cleanup helpers or invoke extension points after construction.

Wrong move: Let one wrapper call another wrapper -> nested wrappers execute the hook twice and duplicate side effects -> instead share private helpers and keep each public operation on a single hook path.
